denomProfiles.tagline: Zulu prophetic church of Isaiah Shembe, centred on Ekuphakameni and the holy mountain Nhlangakazi.
coreDoctrines: God revealed himself afresh to the Zulu people through the prophet Isaiah Shembe, whom members honour as a divinely sent messenger.
Scripture is read alongside Shembe's own hymns and teachings, which carry revelatory authority for members.
Strict observance of a Saturday Sabbath, following Old Testament law.
Healing comes through prayer, the prophet's blessing and obedience rather than medicine or traditional diviners.
Purity laws drawn from the Hebrew Bible govern food, dress and conduct.
focuses: Restoring dignity and order to African life under colonial and apartheid pressure.
Holy places: Ekuphakameni and Nhlangakazi mountain as sacred sites of pilgrimage.
Continuity of leadership in Shembe's line.
Healing and protection from evil.
practices: Annual January pilgrimage to Nhlangakazi and the July festival at Ekuphakameni.
Sacred dance (ukusina) in traditional and distinctive regalia as worship.
Worship barefoot, in white robes, on holy ground.
Singing from the hymnal Izihlabelelo zamaNazaretha composed largely by Isaiah and Galilee Shembe.
Baptism by immersion and a night-time communion with foot-washing.

influencedBy.name: African Native Baptist Church
influencedBy.text: Shembe was baptised in this Black-led Baptist body in 1906 before founding his own church.

influencedBy.name: Zulu tradition
influencedBy.text: Ancestral reverence, dance, regalia and kingship patterns were incorporated and reinterpreted.

influencedBy.name: Hebrew Bible
influencedBy.text: Sabbath, purity and sacrifice-like observances draw directly on Old Testament law.

influenced.name: African Initiated Churches
influenced.text: The amaNazaretha became a classic case study for Bengt Sundkler's typology of 'Zionist' and 'Ethiopian' churches.

influenced.name: Zulu literature and music
influenced.text: Shembe's hymns are recognised as foundational texts of modern isiZulu religious poetry.

denomProfiles.tagline: West African church born of William Wade Harris's 1913–15 preaching tour along the Ivorian coast.
coreDoctrines: One God, proclaimed against fetishes and traditional cult objects, which converts were urged to burn.
Jesus Christ as Saviour and the Bible as God's word, received through Harris's preaching.
Harris as a prophet of the last days, called by the angel Gabriel in a Liberian prison cell (1910).
The Ten Commandments as the basis of Christian life.
Acceptance of polygamous families, which Harris did not require converts to break up.
focuses: Mass conversion and baptism of coastal peoples of Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana.
Rejection of traditional ritual power and sorcery.
A self-governing African church independent of missions.
Preservation of Harris's teaching through preachers and 'apostles'.
practices: Baptism with water as the sign of turning from fetishes to God.
Worship in white robes, with preachers carrying a cross and Bible as Harris did.
Singing of hymns composed in local languages.
Sunday rest and avoidance of alcohol in many congregations.

influencedBy.name: Methodist and Episcopal missions in Liberia
influencedBy.text: Harris was raised Methodist and served as an Episcopal catechist and teacher before his prophetic call.

influencedBy.name: Old Testament prophets
influencedBy.text: Harris modelled himself on Elijah, earning the nickname 'the Black Elijah'.

influenced.name: Methodist Church in Côte d'Ivoire
influenced.text: Many Harris converts joined Methodist missions arriving after 1924, giving that church its base.

influenced.name: African Initiated Churches
influenced.text: A key early prophetic movement in the history of independent African Christianity.

keyFigures.name: John Ahui
keyFigures.role: Harris's appointed successor and organiser of the church

denomProfiles.tagline: Chinese-rooted network holding one church per city, shaped by Watchman Nee and Witness Lee.
coreDoctrines: The church is one in each locality; denominational division is seen as contrary to the New Testament.
Salvation by grace through faith, followed by the believer's growth in the indwelling divine life.
God's economy: God dispensing himself into humanity to build up the Body of Christ.
Witness Lee's teaching that believers become God 'in life and nature but not in the Godhead'.
The Recovery Version of the Bible, with Lee's footnotes, as the movement's standard text.
focuses: Building up the local church as the practical expression of the Body of Christ.
Ministry publishing through Living Stream Ministry and Taiwan Gospel Book Room.
Every member functioning, without a separate clergy.
Spiritual life and the 'inner life' tradition of Nee's writings.
practices: Weekly Lord's Table meeting with breaking of bread.
'Calling on the name of the Lord' and 'pray-reading' Scripture.
Mutual speaking and prophesying in meetings, led by elders rather than pastors.
Large conferences and trainings, such as the semiannual training in Anaheim.

influencedBy.name: Plymouth Brethren
influencedBy.text: Nee drew heavily on Brethren ecclesiology and Darby's writings, and had links with the Exclusive Brethren.

influencedBy.name: Keswick and inner-life writers
influencedBy.text: Jessie Penn-Lewis, Madame Guyon and others shaped Nee's teaching on the cross and the spirit.

influencedBy.name: Margaret E. Barber
influencedBy.text: English missionary in Fuzhou who mentored the young Nee.

influenced.name: Chinese House Churches
influenced.text: Nee's books and the local-church pattern deeply shaped unregistered Chinese Protestantism.

influenced.name: Global evangelical devotion
influenced.text: Nee's 'The Normal Christian Life' and 'The Spiritual Man' became widely read evangelical classics.

keyFigures.name: Witness Lee
keyFigures.role: Co-worker and later leader in Taiwan and the United States (1905–1997)

denomProfiles.inIndia: Local churches meet in a number of Indian cities, and Nee's books circulate widely among Indian evangelical and Brethren readers.

denomProfiles.tagline: China's state-registered Protestant body: self-governing, self-supporting, self-propagating and 'post-denominational'.
coreDoctrines: Historic Protestant faith in the Trinity, Christ's saving work and the authority of the Bible.
The 'three-self' principles of self-government, self-support and self-propagation, freeing Chinese churches from foreign control.
Patriotism and support for the People's Republic as part of Christian witness.
'Theological reconstruction' (from 1998) emphasising love and harmony with socialist society.
Post-denominational unity: former denominational differences are set aside in shared congregations.
focuses: Registered church life under the State Administration for Religious Affairs.
Training of pastors in seminaries such as Nanjing Union Theological Seminary.
Printing Bibles, notably through the Amity Printing Company in Nanjing.
'Sinicisation' of Christianity in line with official policy since 2015.
practices: Sunday worship with sermon, hymns from the Chinese New Hymnal (1983) and prayer.
Both infant and believer's baptism, according to local custom.
Holy Communion celebrated in varied forms inherited from earlier missions.
Women widely ordained as pastors.

influencedBy.name: Henry Venn and Rufus Anderson
influencedBy.text: The nineteenth-century 'three-self' missionary ideal of indigenous churches.

influencedBy.name: Chinese Protestant missions
influencedBy.text: Its congregations inherit Anglican, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist and other mission churches.

influencedBy.name: The Christian Manifesto (1950)
influencedBy.text: Drafted by Wu Yaozong with Zhou Enlai's approval, it set the movement's political course.

influenced.name: Chinese House Churches
influenced.text: Many unregistered congregations defined themselves by refusing to join the TSPM.

influenced.name: Ecumenical post-denominationalism
influenced.text: Its model has been discussed widely in world ecumenical circles.

keyFigures.name: K. H. Ting (Ding Guangxun)
keyFigures.role: Bishop, TSPM chairman and CCC president, leader of 'theological reconstruction'

members.note: Figure for Protestants in China given in the State Council white paper of April 2018; it refers mainly to registered churches and is widely regarded as a minimum.

denomProfiles.tagline: Pentecostal-style Christian commune founded by Jing Dianying in Mazhuang, Shandong.
coreDoctrines: Salvation through Christ alongside a call to share all goods in common, as in Acts 2.
Direct experience of the Holy Spirit through visions, tongues and prophecy.
Self-denial and suffering as the path of discipleship.
Strong expectation of Christ's return.
focuses: Communal living on farms and workshops as one 'family'.
Care for the poor, disabled and outcast.
Indigenous Chinese church life, independent of missions.
Fervent prayer meetings and revival.
practices: Common ownership of property and shared labour.
Long, emotional prayer meetings with weeping, tongues and dancing.
Simple hymns composed by members.
Strict authority of the family head, Jing Dianying.

influencedBy.name: Pentecostal revival in north China
influencedBy.text: Pentecostal missions in Shandong in the 1920s shaped its spirituality.

influencedBy.name: Methodist missions
influencedBy.text: Jing was educated in Methodist mission schools in Shandong.

influenced.name: Chinese House Churches
influenced.text: Former members and its ethos of sacrifice and charismatic prayer fed later unregistered churches.

denomProfiles.tagline: Pentecostals who baptise 'in the name of Jesus' and teach God's oneness rather than three persons.
coreDoctrines: One God who reveals himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit as modes or manifestations, not three persons.
Jesus is the name of God, and the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily.
Water baptism must be by immersion in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 2:38).
Spirit baptism with the evidence of speaking in tongues, which many bodies hold necessary for salvation.
Mainstream trinitarian churches regard this view as a form of modalism and reject it.
focuses: Evangelism and church planting worldwide.
'Holiness standards' of dress and conduct.
Divine healing and spiritual gifts.
Apostolic doctrine of Acts 2:38 as the full new-birth message.
practices: Rebaptism of converts from trinitarian churches in Jesus' name.
Lively worship with tongues, prophecy and altar calls.
Foot washing in some bodies.
Modest dress and uncut hair for women in many churches.

influencedBy.name: Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Emerged within early Pentecostalism after the 1913 Arroyo Seco camp meeting.

influencedBy.name: William Durham's 'finished work'
influencedBy.text: Durham's Christocentric teaching prepared the ground for the 'New Issue'.

influencedBy.name: R. E. McAlister
influencedBy.text: His 1913 sermon on baptism in Jesus' name sparked the controversy.

influenced.name: United Pentecostal Church International
influenced.text: The largest Oneness denomination.

influenced.name: Pentecostal Assemblies of the World
influenced.text: The oldest surviving Oneness body, interracial from its early years.

influenced.name: True Jesus Church
influenced.text: Shares baptism in Jesus' name and Oneness theology.

keyFigures.name: Garfield T. Haywood
keyFigures.role: Bishop and leader of the PAW

keyFigures.name: Andrew D. Urshan
keyFigures.role: Evangelist and theologian of the movement

denomProfiles.inIndia: Oneness churches have a significant presence in North-East India, especially the United Pentecostal Church (North East India) in Mizoram, with smaller congregations in South India.

denomProfiles.tagline: Restorationist church founded by Joseph Smith, holding modern prophets and the Book of Mormon as scripture.
coreDoctrines: The Godhead as three distinct beings: God the Father and Jesus Christ with glorified bodies, and the Holy Ghost.
A 'Great Apostasy' after the apostles, followed by the restoration of priesthood and church through Joseph Smith.
An open canon: the Bible, Book of Mormon, Doctrine and Covenants and Pearl of Great Price, guided by living prophets.
Eternal progression and exaltation: faithful humans may become like God.
Temple ordinances, including eternal marriage and proxy baptism for the dead.
Mainstream Christian churches do not regard its baptism as valid because of its non-Nicene teaching on God.
focuses: Missionary work by tens of thousands of young full-time missionaries.
Family life and the 'eternal family'.
Temple building and family history (genealogy).
Welfare, self-reliance and humanitarian aid.
practices: Sunday sacrament meeting with bread and water blessed by priesthood holders.
Lay priesthood for worthy males from age 11 and a lay ministry of bishops.
Baptism by immersion at age eight or later.
The Word of Wisdom: abstinence from alcohol, tobacco, coffee and tea.
Tithing of ten per cent of income.

influencedBy.name: Burned-over district revivalism
influencedBy.text: Smith grew up amid the revivals and seeker movements of western New York.

influencedBy.name: Primitivist restorationism
influencedBy.text: Like the Stone–Campbell movement, it sought to restore the New Testament church.

influencedBy.name: Freemasonry
influencedBy.text: Scholars note parallels between Masonic ritual and the Nauvoo temple endowment.

influenced.name: Community of Christ
influenced.text: The 'Reorganized' branch that rejected Brigham Young's leadership.

influenced.name: American religious history
influenced.text: A major example of a new religious movement becoming a global church.

keyFigures.name: Brigham Young
keyFigures.role: Second president; led the migration to Utah

members.note: About 17.5 million members on record at the end of 2024, as reported in the Church's statistical report to the April 2025 General Conference.

denomProfiles.inIndia: Present in India since the 1850s with a small modern membership; the India Bengaluru Temple was announced in 2020.

denomProfiles.tagline: Bible-centred movement known for door-to-door preaching and the Watch Tower Society's publications.
coreDoctrines: Jehovah is the one true God; Jesus is his first creation and Son, not God the Son, and the holy spirit is God's active force.
God's Kingdom, ruling invisibly from heaven since 1914, will soon replace human governments at Armageddon.
Only 144,000 'anointed' go to heaven; other faithful people hope to live forever on a paradise earth.
The soul is mortal; there is no hell of eternal torment.
Political neutrality and refusal of blood transfusions as matters of conscience and obedience.
Mainstream churches reject its Christology and its claims for the Governing Body.
focuses: Public preaching from house to house and with literature carts.
Bible study through Watchtower and other publications.
Strict moral discipline within congregations.
Separation from politics, war and interfaith activity.
practices: Meetings at Kingdom Halls twice weekly.
Baptism by immersion of committed adult publishers.
Annual Memorial of Christ's death, with emblems taken only by the anointed.
No celebration of Christmas, Easter or birthdays.
The New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures.

influencedBy.name: Bible Students
influencedBy.text: Grew out of the Bible Student movement of Charles Taze Russell.

influencedBy.name: Adventism
influencedBy.text: Russell drew on Adventist chronologies and conditional immortality.

influencedBy.name: Joseph F. Rutherford
influencedBy.text: Reorganised the movement and adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931.

influenced.name: Religious-liberty law
influenced.text: Witness lawsuits shaped freedom-of-religion law in the United States, Canada and Europe.

influenced.name: Bible Students
influenced.text: Groups that rejected Rutherford's changes continued as independent Bible Students.

keyFigures.name: Charles Taze Russell
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Bible Student movement

keyFigures.name: Joseph F. Rutherford
keyFigures.role: Second president of the Watch Tower Society (1917–1942)

keyFigures.name: Nathan H. Knorr
keyFigures.role: Third president; expanded training and translation

members.note: Peak of just over 9 million active publishers in the 2024 service year, with about 21 million attending the Memorial (Jehovah's Witnesses' own report).

denomProfiles.inIndia: Congregations meet throughout India, with literature in many Indian languages including Tamil and Malayalam; Witnesses were party to the Supreme Court's Bijoe Emmanuel judgment (1986) on the national anthem.

denomProfiles.tagline: Liberal tradition rejecting the Trinity, valuing reason, conscience and freedom of belief.
coreDoctrines: God is one person; Jesus is a uniquely inspired human teacher rather than God incarnate.
Reason and conscience are guides to religious truth alongside Scripture.
Human goodness and moral improvement rather than original sin.
Religious freedom and tolerance, as proclaimed in the Edict of Torda (1568).
In modern Unitarian Universalism, a creedless faith open to many sources beyond Christianity.
focuses: Freedom of thought and toleration.
Social reform: abolition, women's rights, education and civil rights.
Rational and historical study of the Bible.
Democratic congregational life.
practices: Congregational worship with readings, hymns and sermon, often without creeds.
Infant baptism in Transylvanian and some British churches; child dedications in many UU congregations.
Flower Communion, introduced by Norbert Čapek in Prague in 1923.
Ordination of women ministers since the nineteenth century.

influencedBy.name: Polish Brethren and Socinianism
influencedBy.text: The Racovian Catechism (1605) shaped anti-trinitarian theology.

influencedBy.name: Radical Reformation
influencedBy.text: Michael Servetus and other radicals questioned the Trinity.

influencedBy.name: English Presbyterian dissent
influencedBy.text: Many English Unitarian chapels developed from Presbyterian congregations.

influenced.name: Brahmo Samaj
influenced.text: Rammohun Roy corresponded with Unitarians, and Brahmo theism was shaped by these links.

influenced.name: American Transcendentalism
influenced.text: Emerson and Parker emerged from Unitarian circles.

influenced.name: Liberal Protestantism
influenced.text: Unitarian biblical criticism fed wider liberal theology.

keyFigures.name: Francis Dávid
keyFigures.role: Founder of the Transylvanian Unitarian Church

denomProfiles.inIndia: The Khasi Unitarian Union in Meghalaya traces its origins to Hajom Kissor Singh in 1887, and Unitarian ideas influenced the Brahmo Samaj.

denomProfiles.tagline: Oldest continuing Oneness Pentecostal body, historically interracial and led by bishops.
coreDoctrines: One God revealed in Jesus Christ, without distinct persons.
Repentance, baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues as the new birth.
Holiness of life.
Divine healing.
focuses: Evangelism and church planting, especially among African Americans.
Episcopal oversight by a council of bishops.
Holiness and family life.
Overseas missions in Africa, the Caribbean and Asia.
practices: Baptism by immersion in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.
Exuberant worship with gospel music and tongues.
Communion and foot washing.
Women serve as ministers and missionaries, though the episcopate has been male.

influencedBy.name: Azusa Street revival
influencedBy.text: Its earliest leaders came out of the 1906 revival.

influencedBy.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Adopted the 'New Issue' after 1916.

influenced.name: United Pentecostal Church International
influenced.text: White members who left the PAW in 1924 eventually formed bodies that merged into the UPCI.

influenced.name: Gospel music
influenced.text: Haywood's hymns, such as 'Jesus, the Son of God', entered Pentecostal hymnody.

denomProfiles.tagline: Largest Oneness Pentecostal denomination, known for Acts 2:38 preaching and holiness standards.
coreDoctrines: One God, fully revealed in Jesus Christ; the Trinity of persons is rejected.
The new birth is repentance, baptism in Jesus' name and receiving the Holy Spirit with tongues.
Holiness of life, including outward standards of dress.
Divine healing and the premillennial return of Christ.
focuses: Global missions and church planting.
Bible colleges and ministerial training.
Holiness 'standards' and separation from worldliness.
Revival and evangelism.
practices: Baptism by immersion in the name of Jesus.
Spirit-filled worship with tongues, music and altar prayer.
Women generally wear long hair and dresses; television and adornment discouraged historically.
Women may hold a ministerial licence, though senior offices are held by men.

influencedBy.name: Pentecostal Assemblies of the World
influencedBy.text: Its founders came from bodies that left the PAW in 1924.

influencedBy.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Formed in 1945 by merger of the Pentecostal Church, Inc. and the Pentecostal Assemblies of Jesus Christ.

influenced.name: Oneness churches worldwide
influenced.text: Its missionaries founded national United Pentecostal churches in many countries.

keyFigures.name: David K. Bernard
keyFigures.role: General superintendent and theologian of Oneness doctrine

denomProfiles.inIndia: UPCI missionaries work in India, and the separately organised United Pentecostal Church (North East India) is a major denomination in Mizoram.

denomProfiles.tagline: Filipino church holding Felix Manalo as God's last messenger restoring the true church.
coreDoctrines: God the Father is the only true God; Jesus is a man, Son of God and Saviour, but not God.
The original church apostatised; the true Church of Christ re-emerged in the Philippines on 27 July 1914.
Felix Manalo is the 'angel from the east' of Revelation 7 and God's last messenger.
Membership in the Iglesia ni Cristo is necessary for salvation.
Mainstream churches reject its Christology and its claim to be the only true church.
focuses: Unity and discipline under the Executive Minister.
Evangelism and rapid expansion, including abroad.
Large chapel-building programme with distinctive architecture.
Bloc voting in Philippine elections as an expression of unity.
practices: Twice-weekly worship services with set doctrinal lessons.
Baptism by immersion after instruction.
Annual Holy Supper.
Regular offerings and strict attendance.
Marriage to non-members discouraged.

influencedBy.name: Adventist and other Protestant missions
influencedBy.text: Manalo passed through Methodist, Presbyterian, Disciples and Seventh-day Adventist churches.

influencedBy.name: Restorationism
influencedBy.text: Shares the theme of an apostasy and restoration.

influenced.name: Philippine society
influenced.text: Became one of the largest and most influential religious bodies in the Philippines.

members.note: About 2.8 million (roughly 2.6 per cent of the population) in the Philippine Statistics Authority's 2020 census; the church gives no official count.

denomProfiles.tagline: Chinese indigenous Pentecostal church keeping the Sabbath and baptising in Jesus' name.
coreDoctrines: One God, revealed in Jesus Christ; Oneness rather than trinitarian theology.
Five doctrines (with Sabbath and foot washing): Spirit baptism with tongues, water baptism, foot washing, Holy Communion and the Sabbath.
Water baptism by full immersion, face downward, in living water, in the name of Jesus.
The True Jesus Church as the restored church of the latter rain.
Mainstream churches question its exclusive claims and Oneness teaching.
focuses: Saturday Sabbath worship.
Spirit baptism evidenced by tongues.
Evangelism among Chinese communities worldwide.
Self-supporting indigenous church.
practices: Prayer together aloud in tongues, kneeling.
Foot washing as a sacrament.
Holy Communion with one loaf of unleavened bread and grape juice.
Separation of men and women in seating in many congregations.

influencedBy.name: Apostolic Faith Mission
influencedBy.text: Pentecostal missionaries brought tongues and Oneness ideas to north China.

influencedBy.name: Seventh-day Adventism
influencedBy.text: Influenced its Sabbath observance.

influencedBy.name: Oneness Pentecostalism
influencedBy.text: Shares baptism in Jesus' name.

influenced.name: Chinese House Churches
influenced.text: A strand of indigenous Pentecostal piety in Chinese Christianity.

denomProfiles.tagline: Lay-led Bible community awaiting Christ's return to establish God's Kingdom on earth.
coreDoctrines: God is one; Jesus is the Son of God, born of Mary, not pre-existent; the Holy Spirit is God's power.
Humans are mortal; the hope is bodily resurrection, not an immortal soul.
The Kingdom of God will be established on earth, centred on Israel, at Christ's return.
The devil is understood as human sin, not a personal fallen angel.
Belief of the gospel and baptism by immersion are necessary for salvation.
focuses: Bible reading and study, aided by Robert Roberts's daily 'Bible Companion'.
Expectation of Christ's return and attention to prophecy and Israel.
Conscientious objection to military service.
Mutual care within ecclesias.
practices: Weekly 'Breaking of Bread' memorial meeting.
No paid clergy; brothers take turns to preside and exhort.
Baptism of believers by immersion after examination.
Fraternal gatherings and Bible schools.

influencedBy.name: Stone–Campbell movement
influencedBy.text: John Thomas began among the Disciples before breaking away.

influencedBy.name: Millerite Adventism
influencedBy.text: Adventist expectations shaped Thomas's prophetic outlook.

influenced.name: Conditional immortality
influenced.text: An influential voice for mortalism within dissenting Protestantism.

keyFigures.name: Robert Roberts
keyFigures.role: Organiser and editor of The Christadelphian

denomProfiles.tagline: Church founded by Mary Baker Eddy teaching healing through spiritual understanding of God.
coreDoctrines: God is infinite Mind, Spirit, Life, Truth and Love; matter, sin and disease are not ultimately real.
Jesus is the Way-shower who demonstrated the Christ, divine truth, but is not himself God.
Healing comes through prayer that corrects mistaken material belief.
The Bible and Eddy's 'Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures' are the church's pastor.
Mainstream churches reject its denial of the reality of matter and its non-trinitarian theology.
focuses: Spiritual healing in place of medical treatment.
Reading rooms and publishing, including The Christian Science Monitor.
Daily study of the Bible Lesson.
Practitioners who give healing treatment through prayer.
practices: Sunday services with readings from the Bible and Science and Health by lay Readers.
Wednesday testimony meetings sharing healings.
No sacraments with physical elements; baptism and communion are understood spiritually.
Governance by the Church Manual and the Mother Church in Boston.

influencedBy.name: Phineas Parkhurst Quimby
influencedBy.text: Eddy was treated by the mental healer in 1862, though she later disowned his influence.

influencedBy.name: New England Congregationalism
influencedBy.text: Eddy's upbringing shaped her biblical piety.

influenced.name: Unity
influenced.text: The New Thought movement, including Unity, drew on Christian Science ideas.

influenced.name: New Thought
influenced.text: Former Christian Scientists such as Emma Curtis Hopkins spread mental-healing teaching.

denomProfiles.tagline: New Thought movement teaching practical Christianity, positive prayer and the divinity in every person.
coreDoctrines: God is divine Mind, present everywhere and in everyone.
Jesus is the great example of humanity realising the Christ within.
Thoughts and words shape experience; affirmative prayer brings health and prosperity.
Openness to truth in all religions and to reincarnation, which the founders accepted.
focuses: Practical spiritual living and healing.
Prayer ministry through Silent Unity, active since 1890.
Publishing, including the Daily Word.
Inclusive and non-dogmatic community.
practices: Sunday services with music, meditation and a talk.
Affirmations and 'denials' in prayer.
Ordination of women and men as ministers.
Burning bowl and other symbolic rituals rather than sacraments.

influencedBy.name: Christian Science
influencedBy.text: Emma Curtis Hopkins, a former Christian Scientist, taught the Fillmores.

influencedBy.name: New Thought
influencedBy.text: Shares the mental-healing tradition of nineteenth-century America.

influenced.name: Positive-thinking spirituality
influenced.text: Unity's literature spread affirmative prayer widely.

denomProfiles.tagline: Celibate communal society awaiting Christ's Second Appearing, known for ecstatic worship and craftsmanship.
coreDoctrines: Christ's Second Appearing was manifested in Mother Ann Lee and continues in the community of Believers.
God is both male and female, Father and Mother.
Celibacy as the way to overcome the root sin of lust.
Confession of sins to elders as the gateway to new life.
Equality of men and women in leadership.
focuses: Communal life in 'families' and villages.
Simplicity, honest work and fine craftsmanship.
Pacifism and separation from the world.
Hospitality to orphans and seekers.
practices: Worship with singing and dances, from which the name 'Shakers' derives.
Thousands of songs, including 'Simple Gifts' (1848).
Parallel male and female leadership of elders and eldresses.
No sacraments of baptism or communion.

influencedBy.name: Quakers
influencedBy.text: The founders came out of the 'Shaking Quakers' of Manchester.

influencedBy.name: French Prophets
influencedBy.text: Camisard ecstatic prophecy influenced the early group.

influenced.name: American design
influenced.text: Shaker furniture and architecture influenced modern design.

influenced.name: Communal movements
influenced.text: A model for nineteenth-century American utopian communities.

keyFigures.name: Joseph Meacham
keyFigures.role: Organised the communities after Lee's death

denomProfiles.tagline: Church built on the visionary writings of Emanuel Swedenborg about God, heaven and the inner sense of Scripture.
coreDoctrines: God is one person, the Lord Jesus Christ, in whom Father, Son and Holy Spirit are three aspects (a trinity of essentials, not persons).
The Last Judgment took place in the spiritual world in 1757, inaugurating the New Jerusalem.
Scripture has an inner, spiritual sense revealed through Swedenborg.
Salvation requires both faith and charity; life after death continues in heaven or hell according to one's love.
Mainstream churches reject its non-trinitarian theology and its claims for Swedenborg's revelations.
focuses: Study of Swedenborg's writings.
Spiritual regeneration in daily life.
Education, especially at Bryn Athyn in Pennsylvania.
Publishing and translation.
practices: Liturgical Sunday worship.
Baptism of infants and adults.
The Holy Supper as a means of conjunction with the Lord.
Women ordained in the General Convention; not in the General Church.

influencedBy.name: Lutheranism
influencedBy.text: Swedenborg was the son of a Swedish Lutheran bishop.

influencedBy.name: Enlightenment science
influencedBy.text: Swedenborg was a scientist before his visions of 1744–45.

influenced.name: Romantic and Transcendentalist writers

denomProfiles.tagline: Independent heirs of Charles Taze Russell's Bible Student movement, outside the Watch Tower Society.
coreDoctrines: God (Jehovah) is supreme; Jesus is the pre-existent Son, not co-equal; the Trinity is rejected.
A ransom sacrifice and restitution for humanity in a coming earthly kingdom.
Mortality of the soul; no eternal torment.
Russell's 'Divine Plan of the Ages' and prophetic chronology.
focuses: Bible study, especially Russell's 'Studies in the Scriptures'.
Independent ecclesias free of central authority.
Witness through broadcasts and literature.
Christian character development.
practices: Ecclesia meetings with Bible study.
Annual Memorial of Christ's death.
Baptism by immersion.
Conventions organised by groups such as the Dawn Bible Students Association.

denomProfiles.tagline: Herbert W. Armstrong's Sabbath-keeping church, later transformed into an evangelical body.
coreDoctrines: God is a family of two divine beings, Father and Son, into which believers may be born; the Holy Spirit is God's power.
The seventh-day Sabbath and the annual holy days of Leviticus 23 are binding.
British Israelism: the British and Americans descend from the 'lost tribes' of Israel.
Armstrong as God's end-time apostle restoring truth.
These teachings were abandoned by the church under Joseph Tkach Sr in the 1990s.
focuses: Broadcasting through The World Tomorrow and publishing The Plain Truth.
Prophetic interpretation of world events.
Ambassador College education.
Tithing, including second and third tithes.
practices: Saturday Sabbath services.
Observance of Passover, the Feast of Tabernacles and other holy days.
Avoidance of Christmas, Easter and unclean meats.
Baptism by immersion of adults.
